summary: This unit teaches advanced business communication for managers. You will learn to plan messages for different audiences, write clear letters, emails and reports, speak, listen and run meetings and video calls, persuade with credibility, logic and emotion, negotiate and handle conflict, communicate with overseas clients and people with different needs, deliver difficult news, handle media and crisis communication, and stay within honesty, confidentiality and data protection limits.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. It is for supervisors and managers who speak and write for their organisation: to staff, customers, suppliers, partners, officials and the media. A manager's words can win a contract or lose one, calm a crisis or start a rumour. The skill is to choose the right message, channel and tone for each audience, and to stay honest.
Communication is **successful when the receiver understands the message as the sender meant it**. That is why a manager checks understanding instead of assuming it.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Decide purpose, audience, channel, tone and timing; write a communication plan for a launch or a change.
Produce clear letters, emails, reports and press releases in the right register, with correct layout and proofreading.
Use active listening and open questions, read body language, present the main point first and run video calls well.
Use credibility, logic and emotion; structure a message with AIDA; end with a clear call to action.
Prepare with interests, BATNA and a walk-away point; look for trade-offs; choose a suitable conflict style.
Prepare for overseas clients, people with disabilities, other languages and community groups.
Handle difficult news, media and crisis
Break bad news with respect, keep confidences, name one spokesperson, issue a prompt accurate statement and manage rumours.
Respect ethical and legal limits and evaluate
Keep claims true, protect confidential and personal information, and check that communication worked.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** with scenarios on channels, writing, persuasion, negotiation, crisis and ethics.
A **written paper** with short answers (BATNA, ZOPA, AIDA, register, jargon, grapevine) and essays.
**Practical group work**: preparing for and holding a supplier negotiation and confirming it in writing, then preparing a crisis communication pack and holding a mock media interview.

blocks.note: Be ready to give the exact term and to apply it to a situation. For example, you may be asked what BATNA means and also to work out a walk-away point.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: The communication process, audiences and channels

flow: Sender: has an idea and decides its purpose
Message: the idea put into words, numbers, pictures or tone
Channel: the way it is sent (talk, call, letter, email, report, notice, social media)
Receiver: the person who gets the message and gives it meaning
Feedback: the receiver's response, which shows whether the message was understood

blocks.p: **Noise** is anything that distorts or blocks the message: a bad phone line, background chatter, jargon, a rude tone, stress, or the receiver's own assumptions. Good senders reduce noise and ask for feedback.

head: Barrier
Example
How to overcome it
rows: A client speaks another language, or does not know the technical terms
Plain words; explain terms; use a qualified interpreter or translator
Different customs on greetings, directness, time and rank
Research the culture; ask politely when unsure
Poor phone or internet link, noise, distance
Test equipment early; choose a quiet place; send a written summary
Stay calm; pause; let the person speak; return to facts
"Throughput" and other specialist words used with outsiders
Use everyday words; explain any term you need
Put the main point first; use headings and short paragraphs

blocks.p: The same facts need different messages for different people. If Patrice must tell her bank, her staff and a key client about the same production delay, she keeps the facts the same but changes the content, tone and detail for each. The bank wants the effect on repayments; the staff want to know about their jobs and work; the client wants the new delivery date and what is being done.

head: Channel
Best for
Weaknesses
rows: Sensitive news, building trust, quick back-and-forth
No record unless you follow up in writing
Quick, short updates; confirming arrangements; sending documents
Can seem casual; easy to forward; long emails get skimmed; tone is hard to judge
Serious matters; formal replies; contracts and official bodies
Detailed findings and recommendations for decision makers
Time to write; must be well organised
Information for many people in one place
One-way; some people will miss it or cannot read it
Technical problems; harder to read body language
Reaching many customers quickly; quick updates
Posts spread fast and are hard to take back; risks to privacy and reputation

blocks.note: A good rule: use **a call first, then an email to confirm** when news is important and the relationship matters. Bad news that needs a personal talk should not be given only by email.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: When a change affects several groups, such as a new service that staff, clients and suppliers must hear about, write a **communication plan**: a table showing **who** is told **what**, **how** and **when**, and who is responsible.

head: Audience
Key message
Channel
When
Who
rows: What is changing and what it means for their work
The new service and how to use it

blocks.p: **Plain language** uses everyday words, short sentences and a clear structure so that readers understand the message the first time. Write "Please pay within 14 days of receiving this letter" instead of "Remittance is requested within a fortnight of receipt of the present correspondence." Plain language is not childish; it is respect for the reader's time.

ul: Put the **main point first**.
Use headings, short paragraphs, bullet points and numbered steps.
Use the active voice: "We will deliver on Friday", not "Delivery will be made."
Be specific: dates, amounts and names, not "soon" or "some time".
Explain terms and avoid jargon with outside readers.

blocks.p: **Register** is the level of formality of language suited to the situation. A letter to the permanent secretary of a ministry needs a formal, courteous register. A quick message to a colleague you work with daily can be informal. Match the register to the reader and the purpose.

head: Part
Notes
rows: At the top, on letterhead where the firm has it
Check spelling of names and titles
Dear Mrs Lewis (named person); Dear Sir or Madam (no name known)
Opening: why you are writing. Middle: the facts and what you want. End: what happens next
**Yours sincerely** after a named greeting; **Yours faithfully** after Dear Sir or Madam
Sign above the typed name and job title

blocks.p: Before an important letter goes out, **proofread** it and ask a colleague to check it. A spelling error in a letter to an official or a client harms the firm's image.

ul: Use a clear subject line and a short message with the action and date.
Use a polite greeting and closing, and a professional tone. Do not use capital letters for shouting.
When writing to many outside people, put their addresses in the **Bcc** line so each person's address is not shown to the others. This protects privacy.
Re-read before sending: you cannot recall a mistake once it is out.
If you receive a rude email, wait, then reply calmly and keep to the facts. Do not reply in anger.

blocks.p: A formal business report usually follows this order: title page; summary; introduction; method; findings; conclusions; **recommendations** (placed **after** the conclusions, because they follow from them); appendices. Busy readers need headings, short paragraphs and a summary on the first page. Use a **line graph** to show how something changed over time (for example sales over 12 months), a **bar chart** to compare amounts, and a **table** for exact figures.

A **press release** is a short written statement sent to news outlets to announce news. The first paragraph answers **who, what, when, where and why**. Then add a quotation, background and a contact name for questions. Keep it factual: do not make claims you cannot prove.

ul: Use people-first language: **visitors with disabilities**, not "the disabled".
Avoid words that assume gender, age or background unless they are needed.
Write notices in plain words and consider large print and other formats.
Do not use slang, jokes or phrases that can hurt or exclude.

blocks.p: Active listening means giving your full attention and showing that you have understood. In a difficult meeting with a client, an active listener does these things:

ul: Looks at the speaker, does not interrupt and puts the phone away.
**Summarises** the client's points and checks understanding: "So the main problem is the late deliveries and the lack of notice. Is that right?"
Asks questions to clear up what is not clear.
Notes the feelings as well as the facts.

head: Type
Example
Use
rows: What problems do you have with your current system?
Do you need delivery on Fridays?
Can you tell me more about what happened on Tuesday?
Wouldn't you agree this is the best option?

blocks.p: **Body language** is communication through posture, gesture, eye contact and facial expression. Folded arms, looking away and short answers may show a worry, but they can also mean tiredness, so do not assume. In a video call, if a client shows such signs, pause and ask whether he has any concern. Keep your own body language open and your tone calm.

ol: Start with **the main point and what you need from them** (a decision, approval, funds).
Give the three or four reasons, with evidence.
Show the options and the risks.
Repeat the request and the next step.
Allow time for questions and keep to the time you were given.

blocks.p: Plan your words for the time you have. If you speak at about 125 words a minute, an 8-minute talk is about 1,000 words. Use plain words and explain any term you need, especially with a community audience, for example when a technical manager speaks to a group in a rural parish.

ul: Test the link and your sound early; join a few minutes before the start.
Use a plain, tidy background and look at the camera when you speak.
Mute when not speaking; avoid side conversations.
Check time zones and public holidays when fixing a time. Jamaica does not change its clocks, but many countries do, so the gap changes during the year.
Send a short written summary after the call.

blocks.p: An **elevator pitch** is a short spoken summary of who you are and what you offer, lasting about 30 seconds. Practise it for networking events and chance meetings. After you meet a useful contact at a business chamber event, send a **short personal email within a few days** to follow up.

head: Style
Example
rows: "Sorry to trouble you, whenever you have time, maybe the report..."
"You are always late with reports. Do it properly for once."
"I need the report by Thursday for the board. Please tell me today if that is a problem."

blocks.note: Assertive means clear, direct and respectful: you state what you need and why, and you listen to the answer.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: To persuade is to help people choose to act, by giving them good reasons. A manager persuades a director to approve a new process, a board to fund a project, a client to sign. Ethical persuasion uses true facts and a fair appeal.

head: Appeal
What it is
Example
Use with care
rows: The speaker is believable: knowledge, experience, honesty
A manager who has run a small pilot, or who brings in a respected expert
Without credibility, good figures may be doubted
Reasons and evidence: figures, results, comparisons
"The pilot cut packing time from 12 to 8 minutes a carton"
Most important with a board that must justify spending
Values and feelings: fairness, safety, pride, concern for people
A short story of a customer's problem
Must be true and fair; do not exploit fear

blocks.p: Most strong messages use all three, with **logic** carrying the most weight in a business case and **credibility** as the foundation.

flow: Attention: open with something that makes the reader care, such as a fact about a problem
Interest: show how the problem affects them and how big it is
Desire: show the solution and its benefits, with evidence
Action: tell them exactly what to do next

blocks.p: The **call to action** at the end tells the reader the next step to take: "Please approve the J$900,000 for the pilot at Friday's meeting." A message without one leaves the reader unsure of what to do.

When a manager wants her director to approve a new process, she links it to the director's goals, with evidence: how it reduces cost, saves time, cuts errors or improves service, with figures from a pilot or from other firms. She prepares for objections and offers options, and she does not use pressure or surprise.

blocks.note: Do not exaggerate. A claim that cannot be checked can destroy credibility the first time it is questioned.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A negotiation is a discussion in which two sides try to reach an agreement. Good negotiators prepare before they meet.

flow: Gather facts: what you buy or sell, past prices, market prices, the other side's likely reasons
Decide your **interests** (what you really need) as opposed to your **positions** (what you say you want)
Work out your **BATNA**: your best alternative to a negotiated agreement
Decide your **walk-away point**: the worst deal you will accept, set from your BATNA
Guess the other side's interests and BATNA
Prepare **trade-offs**: things you can give that cost you little but matter to them
Meet, listen, explore options and agree; confirm the agreement in writing

head: Term
Meaning
rows: What a party says it wants ("payment in 7 days")
The reason behind the position ("we need cash to buy seed at planting time")
Best alternative to a negotiated agreement: what you will do if no deal is reached. It tells you when to walk away from a poor deal
Zone of possible agreement: the range in which both sides' acceptable outcomes overlap
The limit beyond which you prefer your BATNA
Giving something to gain something else

blocks.p: A buyer will pay up to 6% more for supplies, and a supplier wants at least 4%. The ZOPA is 4% to 6%. If the buyer's BATNA is another supplier at 5% more, then any deal above 5% is worse than the alternative, so the buyer's real walk-away point is 5%, and the ZOPA is 4% to 5%.

blocks.note: Do not start with your best offer, and never reveal your walk-away point. But do listen: the other side's interest, such as a cash-flow worry, often points to a cheap solution, such as a faster payment date in return for a smaller price rise.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Seek options that meet both sides' main interests

blocks.p: A win-win approach keeps a long-term partner. If a supplier insists on payment within 15 days and the buyer wants 60, ask why. If the supplier's worry is cash flow, there may be a middle path: part payment earlier and the rest later, a short supply contract in return for earlier payment, or a small early-payment discount. Threats and take-it-or-leave-it offers damage the relationship.

head: Style
What it is
Best when
rows: A real emergency or safety issue needs an immediate decision
Working together for a solution that meets both sides' needs
The issue matters and the relationship matters, such as between two partner firms
The issue is moderate and time is short
The issue is trivial or emotions are too high, so a pause helps
Giving way to the other side
The issue matters more to them than to you, and the relationship matters

blocks.h: A difficult conversation with a partner

ul: Collect the facts: the agreed standard in the contract, and specific examples with dates and the effect on your business.
Decide the outcome you want, such as a recovery plan in a month, and what you will do if it is not met.
Arrange a private meeting and say the purpose in advance.
Explain, listen and agree actions, owners and dates. Follow up in writing.

sections.title: Communicating across cultures and with different needs

ul: **Research** their business customs: greetings and titles, formal or informal style, how direct they are, attitudes to time and who decides.
Speak clearly and avoid local slang, idioms and jokes that may not translate.
**Confirm key points in writing**, because written English is easier to follow than fast speech.

Check **time zones** and public holidays when arranging calls. For example, in January the United Kingdom is 5 hours ahead of Jamaica; in the northern summer it is 6 hours ahead, because the UK changes its clocks and Jamaica does not.
Use the buyer's preferred formal titles until invited to use first names.
Be punctual and prepare the meeting plan.

blocks.note: A first meeting with buyers from another country is not the time to guess. Learn their business customs and plan the meeting carefully.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.h: People with disabilities and different needs

ul: Ask people what help they need instead of assuming.
Provide information in several forms: plain text, large print, spoken announcements, and a sign-language interpreter for deaf people where needed.
Make meeting places accessible, and describe visuals aloud for people who cannot see them.
Speak to the person, not to their companion.
Use respectful, people-first language.

blocks.p: If a manager must hold a detailed discussion with a client who speaks only another language, the best choice is a **qualified interpreter**, not a friend who speaks a little of it: mistakes in a contract or a safety message can be serious. In a community meeting, use plain words, explain any term and invite questions.

Business chambers, trade fairs and associations give contacts and early news. After meeting someone useful, send a short personal email within a few days and propose a next step. Keep promises, and share useful information with your contacts.

head: Benefits
Risks
Sensible rules
rows: Posts spread fast and are hard to remove
Public complaints can grow if handled badly
Named staff only speak for the firm
Reply to complaints publicly and with care, then move to a private channel
Check facts and tone before posting

sections.title: Difficult messages, the media and crisis communication

blocks.p: Bad news that affects a relationship should usually be given in person or by phone, with a written confirmation. A manager who must tell a long-serving supplier that its contract will not be renewed should meet them, give clear reasons and thank them for their work. Do not hide behind email or delay the news until it leaks.

If a client tells you in confidence about a plan that is not public, such as closing a branch, you must **keep it confidential as agreed**, even if the information would help your own firm. Breaking a confidence destroys trust. Share confidential information only with those who need to know and have the right to know.

The **grapevine** is the informal, unofficial spread of information and rumour in an organisation. It grows fast when people are worried and do not know the facts. If rumours spread about job cuts, management should give staff accurate information as soon as it can, even if the answer is "We do not know yet, and we will update you on Friday." Silence invites speculation.

A **crisis** is a serious event, such as a fire, an accident, a contamination scare or a data loss, that threatens people, the business or its name. Firms prepare a **crisis communication plan** in advance.

flow: Protect people first, and inform the authorities that must be told
Gather the facts; form a small crisis team; do not guess
Name one **authorised spokesperson**; everyone else passes media calls to that person
Issue a short **holding statement** soon, even if you do not yet know everything
Tell staff, customers and others who are directly affected before, or at the same time as, the media
Update regularly at the times you promised
After the crisis, review what worked and update the plan

head: Principle
What it means
rows: Speak early; silence lets others tell the story
Say only what you know; do not speculate about causes or blame
Express care for anyone affected before defending the firm
The same facts to every audience
If you do not know something, say so and say when you will find out

blocks.p: A holding statement says what is known, shows concern, says what is being done and when the next update will be given. For example, after a fire at a warehouse: "A fire broke out at our warehouse overnight. No one was injured. We are working with the fire service and will contact every customer whose delivery is affected by Friday."

ul: A junior officer who is called by a reporter should **pass the call to the authorised spokesperson**, politely and promptly, and not guess or give an opinion.
The spokesperson prepares three key messages, answers questions briefly and truthfully, and does not say "no comment" when there is something safe to say.
Never speak "off the record" in a crisis; assume anything may be quoted.

blocks.p: When a customer posts a complaint, reply publicly with care and politeness, show that the firm has noticed, and then move to a private channel such as a call or direct message to sort out details. Do not argue in public and do not delete criticism unless it breaks the rules.

sections.title: Ethics, legal limits and checking that it worked

blocks.p: A manager who speaks for the business can bind it and affect its reputation. Several limits apply.

head: Limit
What it means
rows: Claims about products, prices, results and approvals must be true and supported. Misleading customers is unfair, may break consumer protection rules and destroys trust. If asked to write that a product is 'approved' by an authority when it is not, refuse and keep every claim true and checkable
Keep client, partner, staff and the firm's own sensitive information safe; share only with those who need it

Personal information must be used for the purpose it was collected for, with consent where needed, and stored safely. Before using a list for a new purpose such as a marketing email, check consent and purpose
No discrimination, harassment or defamation; do not make unproved statements about a person or firm
Speak only on matters you are authorised to speak on; pass media calls to the spokesperson
Keep important messages and agreements in writing

blocks.note: Refer to these laws by their purpose, such as the data protection law, consumer protection and defamation rules. If unsure, ask your manager or legal adviser before sending.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Do not assume that a message was understood. Check:

ul: **Ask for feedback:** invite questions, ask people to say in their own words what they will do.
**Follow up:** a short survey, a call or a meeting after an important message.
**Measure:** for a newsletter, track opens, replies and client feedback; for a notice, count attendance or enquiries.
**Adjust:** change the message, channel or timing if the response is poor.

blocks.p: A final point: communication is a core management skill. Good managers prepare, speak plainly, listen more than they talk, keep their word and keep confidences.

ul: describe the communication process and name barriers and noise.
adapt content, tone and channel for each audience.
write a communication plan showing who is told what, how and when.
write letters, emails, reports and press releases in plain language and the right register.
use Dear Sir or Madam with Yours faithfully, and a named greeting with Yours sincerely.
use active listening and open questions, and read body language carefully.
present to senior people with the main point first, and run a video call properly.
persuade with credibility, logic and emotion, and structure a message with AIDA and a call to action.
prepare for a negotiation with interests, BATNA, ZOPA, a walk-away point and trade-offs.
choose a conflict style to suit the situation.
communicate with overseas clients, people with disabilities and speakers of other languages.
give bad news, keep confidences and manage rumours.
plan crisis communication with one spokesperson and a prompt, accurate holding statement.
keep communication honest, lawful and respectful of data protection, and check that it worked.

terms: Anything that distorts or blocks a message.
The receiver's response back to the sender.
Everyday words, short sentences and a clear structure.
The level of formality of language suited to the situation.
Specialist words that outsiders may not understand.
Communication through posture, gesture and facial expression.
Giving full attention and showing you have understood, for example by summarising.
Attention, interest, desire, action: a persuasive sequence.
The closing statement that tells the reader the next step.
Best alternative to a negotiated agreement.
Zone of possible agreement: the range where both sides' acceptable outcomes overlap.
The limit beyond which you prefer your alternative to a deal.
People or groups with an interest in, or affected by, an organisation's work.
The informal, unofficial spread of information and rumour.
A short written statement sent to news outlets to announce news.
A short early statement that says what is known and what is being done.
The plan prepared in advance for communicating when something goes seriously wrong.
A short spoken summary of who you are and what you offer.

c1.title: A restaurant and a farmers' co-operative
c1.text: Andrea Campbell owns a restaurant in Montego Bay. She buys vegetables worth J$500,000 a month from a farmers' co-operative and pays 30 days after delivery. The co-operative asks for a price rise of 8% and payment within 7 days, because members need cash for seed at planting time. Andrea can accept a rise of up to 5%. A second grower would supply at 3% more than the current price, but its deliveries are less reliable.

c2.title: A warehouse fire in Spanish Town
c2.text: A building-materials distributor in Spanish Town has a fire in its warehouse overnight. No one is hurt. Deliveries to about 60 customers will be late. At 8:00 a.m. a radio reporter telephones the receptionist for information. Staff arriving at work are already saying that the business will close, and photos of the fire are on social media.

c3.title: A market relocation notice
c3.text: A municipal corporation in Jamaica must move vendors from the old market building to a new block while repairs are made. Mrs Gayle, the communications officer, must write a notice and hold a meeting. Some vendors do not read well, and one vendor has a hearing impairment. The vendors need to know where their new stalls are and the date to move.

c4.title: A video call with buyers in London
c4.text: Camille Brown works for a Kingston spice exporter. She must hold a video call with buyers in London in January. The call is set for 9:00 a.m. Jamaica time. Later she must ask her own board to approve a new packing machine. A pilot machine cut packing time from 12 minutes to 8 minutes a carton.

c5.title: A distribution firm in Hanover
c5.text: Marlon Pryce manages a distribution firm in Lucea, Hanover. Rumours are spreading that the firm will close its branch. Marlon must also deal with a courier partner whose vehicles have been late on 9 of the last 40 deliveries. Yesterday a fuel leak at the depot created a safety hazard that needed an immediate decision about evacuating the yard.

questions.q: What is Andrea's BATNA in the negotiation?
o: Accepting the co-operative's rise of 8%
Buying from the second grower at 3% more
Paying the co-operative within 7 days
Refusing to talk until the rise is dropped
questions.why: The BATNA is the best alternative if no deal is reached. The second grower at 3% more is her alternative, and it also sets her walk-away point against any offer above that.

questions.q: What is the co-operative's real interest behind its demand for payment in 7 days?
o: Having a shorter contract with the restaurant
Making more profit from every sale
Reducing the number of its deliveries
Having cash at planting time to buy seed
questions.why: The position is "payment in 7 days"; the interest is cash for seed. Knowing the interest lets Andrea look for other ways to meet it, such as an earlier part-payment.

questions.q: Which proposal best seeks a deal that meets both sides' main interests?
o: A 4% rise, 14-day payment and a six-month contract
No rise at all, and payment kept at 30 days
An 8% rise and payment in 7 days to keep the peace
A warning that she will switch grower unless they agree
questions.why: The offer gives the co-operative faster cash and steady orders, and keeps Andrea inside her 5% limit. Refusing everything or giving way entirely fails one side, and a threat damages the relationship.

questions.q: If a 6% rise is agreed on the J$500,000 monthly purchases, how much more will she pay in a year?
questions.why: 6% of 500,000 = J$30,000 a month. Over 12 months that is 30,000 × 12 = J$360,000. J$30,000 is only one month, and J$480,000 would be an 8% rise.

questions.q: The reporter phones the receptionist at 8:00 a.m. What should she do?
o: Tell the reporter what she saw when she arrived
Say that the firm has no comment and hang up
Pass the call to the authorised spokesperson
Give the reporter the manager's mobile phone number
questions.why: Only the authorised spokesperson speaks to the media, so that the facts are accurate and consistent. A junior officer who guesses can spread wrong information, and refusing rudely looks like hiding something.

questions.q: Which is the best content for the first public statement?
o: What is known, concern for people and the action taken
The cause of the fire and who was to blame
A promise that all deliveries will be on time next week
Nothing, until the insurance company has reported
questions.why: A holding statement should be prompt and accurate and show concern. Speculating about the cause or making promises you may not keep damages credibility, and waiting for days lets rumours fill the gap.

questions.q: How should the firm contact the 60 customers whose deliveries are late?
o: Post a notice on social media and let them find it
Wait until each customer phones to complain
Send one email, with all addresses visible, to all of them
Call them directly and confirm the new dates in writing
questions.why: Customers directly affected should hear from the firm first, in a personal way, with a written confirmation of the new dates. A public post may be missed and an email showing every address breaches privacy.

questions.q: Staff are saying that the business will close. What should management do?
o: Say nothing until the rumours stop by themselves
Brief staff soon, with the facts that are known
Tell staff to ignore the rumours and return to work
Warn staff that anyone who talks about it will be disciplined
questions.why: Rumours grow when people do not know the facts. Honest, early information, including what is not yet known, builds trust. Silence, orders and threats leave the grapevine in charge.

questions.q: Which sentence is best for the vendors' notice?
o: Vendors are requested to effect relocation to Block C forthwith.
Please move to Block C by Friday 14 June.
Move or lose your stall.
The move will take place at some time soon.
questions.why: Plain language uses everyday words, a clear action, a place and a date. Formal jargon is hard to read, a threat is not respectful, and a vague time leaves vendors unsure.

questions.q: How should Mrs Gayle reach vendors who do not read well?
o: Post one notice at the gate and leave it up
Post a long written letter to every single vendor
Add spoken announcements and a face-to-face meeting
Ask the vendors to read the council's website for details
questions.why: Using more than one channel, with spoken information, reaches people who cannot read well. One written notice may be missed or not understood.

questions.q: What should be arranged for the vendor with a hearing impairment?
o: A sign-language interpreter at the meeting
A seat at the back so that he is not in the way
A friend who speaks louder when he is nearby
Nothing, as the notice will be posted
questions.why: Ask what help is needed and provide it, so that the person receives the same information as everyone else. A louder voice or a seat at the back does not help someone who cannot hear.

questions.q: Which visual best helps vendors to find their new stalls?
o: A table of the council's budget for the repairs
A bar chart of the number of vendors by year
A photo of the old market building
A map of the new block with stalls numbered
questions.why: A clear map answers the question the vendors will ask. Budget tables, charts and old photos are not useful for the purpose.

questions.q: What time will it be in London when the call starts?
questions.why: In January London is on GMT, which is 5 hours ahead of Jamaica (Jamaica is UTC−5 all year). 9:00 a.m. + 5 hours = 2:00 p.m. In summer the gap is 6 hours because London changes its clocks.

questions.q: How should Camille speak to the London buyers?
o: Quickly and informally, using local expressions to build friendship
Clearly, avoiding slang, and confirming key points in writing
Slowly and loudly, repeating each sentence three times
Only in short answers, leaving the buyers to ask questions
questions.why: Slang may not be understood, and writing is easier to follow than fast speech. Speaking very slowly and loudly can seem disrespectful, and short answers leave the buyers without the information they need.

questions.q: Which opening is the best 'attention' step for her board pitch?
o: We would like to talk about a new machine today
Good morning, and thank you all for coming today
Last month we lost three orders to slow packing
Packing machines are made in many countries
questions.why: AIDA opens with something that makes the reader care. A concrete, costly problem gets attention. A greeting and a general remark do not.

questions.q: Which remark is a fair appeal to emotion for the board?
o: Packers strain their backs on cartons, and this would protect them
The machine would pay for itself within about fourteen months
I have managed the packing section of this firm for over ten years
The pilot cut packing time from twelve to eight minutes a carton
questions.why: An appeal to emotion speaks to values such as the safety and wellbeing of people, and must be true and fair. The payback figure and the pilot result are appeals to logic, and her years of experience support credibility.

questions.q: How should Marlon deal with the rumour about closing the branch?
o: Give staff the facts as soon as he can
Deny it at once without knowing the facts
Ignore it until someone asks him directly
Leave the owner to announce it when it is final
questions.why: Staff need facts early, even "we do not know yet, and we will update you Friday". Denying without facts risks losing trust, and silence feeds the grapevine.

questions.q: Which conflict style fits the fuel-leak hazard that needed an immediate decision?
o: Avoiding
Compromising
Accommodating
Competing
questions.why: In an emergency, one person decides quickly, which is the competing style. Avoiding or compromising wastes time when safety is at risk.

questions.q: Before the meeting with the courier partner, what should Marlon decide?
o: Which of his staff he would like to blame
The result he wants and his next step if refused
How to keep the discussion short, without examples
Whether to hold the meeting by email only
questions.why: A difficult conversation needs a clear goal, such as a recovery plan in a month, and a plan if the partner does not deliver. Blame, no facts and avoiding a face-to-face meeting reduce the chance of a solution.

questions.q: A manager has 8 minutes for a talk and speaks at about 125 words a minute. About how many words should her talk contain?
o: 250 words
1,500 words
1,000 words
16 words
questions.why: 8 minutes × 125 words = 1,000 words. Check: 1,000 ÷ 125 = 8 minutes. Keep to the time you are given and leave room for questions.
